Understanding the Symptom: Vomiting
A general health awareness reference (not a diagnosis)
Symptom Overview
Vomiting means the stomach forcefully brings up its contents through the mouth. It is not a disease by itself — it is a sign that the body is reacting to something, such as an infection, food problem, motion, heat, or another illness. Vomiting can happen once or many times, and it may occur along with other symptoms like loose motion (diarrhoea), fever, stomach pain, weakness, or dizziness. In most cases vomiting settles on its own within a day or two, but sometimes it can lead to loss of body fluids and salts, which needs attention, especially in small children, elderly people, and pregnant women.
Possible Common Causes
Vomiting can happen for many different reasons. This list only describes possible everyday causes — it does not diagnose any illness. A doctor or health worker should be consulted to know the exact cause.
Eating spoiled, stale, or contaminated food or drinking unsafe water
Stomach infections such as viral or bacterial gastroenteritis, which often also cause loose motion
Overeating, eating very oily or spicy food, or eating too fast
Motion sickness during travel by bus, car, or boat
Heat exhaustion or dehydration during hot weather
Pregnancy, especially in the early months (morning sickness)
Fever-related illness, including seasonal infections
Migraine or severe headache
Side effect of certain medicines
Emotional stress, anxiety, or strong smells
Self-Care Advice
If vomiting is mild and the person is otherwise alert and able to drink fluids, simple home care often helps:
Sip small amounts of water, ORS (Oral Rehydration Solution), or clean fluids frequently — do not drink a large amount at once, as this can trigger more vomiting
If ORS packets are available, mix as per the instructions on the packet and drink slowly through the day
If ORS is not available, a simple home fluid can be made using clean water with a little salt and sugar
Rest and avoid solid food for a few hours; once vomiting slows down, start with light food like rice water, banana, toast, or khichdi
Avoid oily, spicy, or heavy food until the stomach settles
For infants, continue breastfeeding; offer small sips of ORS in between feeds
Maintain hand hygiene and keep drinking water covered and clean to avoid spreading infection to others
Take rest in a cool, shaded place, especially during hot weather
When to Seek Medical Attention
Please visit the nearest health centre, sub-centre, or hospital without delay if any of the following are noticed:
⚠ Vomiting continues repeatedly for more than a day, or the person cannot keep any fluids down
⚠ Signs of dehydration: very little or no urine, dry mouth, sunken eyes, extreme thirst, or in infants, no tears when crying and a sunken soft spot on the head
⚠ Blood in the vomit, or vomit that looks like coffee grounds
⚠ Severe stomach pain, high fever, or stiffness in the neck
⚠ Confusion, unusual drowsiness, fainting, or difficulty waking up
⚠ Vomiting after a head injury or fall
⚠ Vomiting in a small child, elderly person, or pregnant woman that does not improve quickly
⚠ Suspected poisoning or reaction after taking any medicine
These signs may point to a more serious condition and need to be checked by a qualified doctor or health worker as soon as possible.
Odisha-Specific Notes
In Odisha, cases of vomiting and loose motion tend to rise during the summer heatwave months and again during the monsoon season. Extreme heat can cause dehydration, weakness, and vomiting, so drinking enough water, ORS, and lemon water, avoiding outdoor work during peak afternoon hours, and eating water-rich fruits are commonly advised during this period. During the monsoon, contaminated drinking water and poor sanitation can lead to outbreaks of diarrhoeal illness in some districts, and local health authorities may issue special alerts. If vomiting occurs along with watery loose motion during such a period, especially if several people in the same household or village fall sick together, it is important to inform the local ASHA worker, sub-centre, or Primary Health Centre (PHC) promptly and to drink only boiled or safely treated water. Free ORS and basic treatment are usually available at government health facilities.
Source Basis
This document is based on general public health guidance from the World Health Organization (WHO), India's Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW), the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), the National Health Mission (NHM), and seasonal health advisories issued by the Government of Odisha's Health Department. It reflects widely accepted general awareness principles on oral rehydration, dehydration recognition, and seasonal illness and is not drawn from any single document.
Sources referred to: World Health Organization (who.int) · Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India (mohfw.gov.in) · Indian Council of Medical Research (icmr.gov.in) · National Health Mission (nhm.gov.in) · Government of Odisha, Department of Health & Family Welfare · Ministry of Ayush / DGHS heatwave advisory.
This content is for general awareness only and does not replace professional medical advice.
